t.3.72.1: Go, Keśinī, and find out who this driver of the chariot is, seated on the chariot's seat, misshapen and short-armed.
t.3.72.2: Approaching him, good lady, attentive and speaking gently at first, you should ask this man about his welfare, and learn the truth of the matter, O blameless one.
t.3.72.3: Here a great suspicion arises in me that this may be King Nala; and so too there is satisfaction in my mind and contentment in my heart.
t.3.72.4: And at the end of your conversation you should repeat to him the words of Parṇāda exactly as they were spoken; and, O lovely-hipped, blameless one, you should take careful note of his reply.
t.3.72.5: Bṛhadaśva said: Thus instructed and attentive, the messenger went and spoke to Bāhuka, while the lovely Damayantī, standing in the palace, watched closely.
t.3.72.6: Welcome to you, lord of men; I wish you well. Hear now, bull among men, the good words of Damayantī.
t.3.72.7: When indeed did you set out, and for what purpose have you come here? Tell this properly, for Vaidarbhī wishes to hear it.
t.3.72.8: The illustrious king of Kosala heard, O lovely lady, that a second svayaṃvara was being held by Damayantī, and that it would take place tomorrow.
t.3.72.9: Having heard that, the king set out with excellent horses swift as the wind, able to travel a hundred yojanas, and I was his charioteer.
t.3.72.10: And that third one among you, where is he from, and whose man is he? And you, whose man are you, and how has this task been entrusted to you?
t.3.72.12: I too am skilled with horses and well accomplished in the work of a cook; Ṛtuparṇa himself has chosen me for the office of charioteer and for the preparation of food.
t.3.72.11: The charioteer of Puṇyaśloka was renowned as Vārṣṇeya; when the noble Nala had fled, he went to Bhāṅgasvari.
t.3.72.13: Now, does Vārṣṇeya know where King Nala has gone? Or perhaps, O Bāhuka, it may somehow have been told to you by him.
t.3.72.15: And no other man knows Nala, O glorious lady; the lord of the earth wanders hidden in this world, his form lost.
t.3.72.14: Having left the two children of Nala, the doer of ill-fated deeds, right here, he then went away as he pleased; he does not know where the Naiṣadha is.
t.3.72.16: For only his own self knows Nala, and she who is closest to him; those signs never at any time proclaim Nala.
t.3.72.17: That brahmin who first went to Ayodhyā at that time, repeating again and again these words of the woman,
t.3.72.18: Where have you gone, O gambler, after cutting off half of my garment, abandoning in the forest your sleeping, devoted beloved, O beloved one?
t.3.72.19: She, just as she was instructed, waits there in expectation of you, burning with grief day and night, wrapped in half a garment.
t.3.72.20: O king, be gracious to her, who weeps constantly from that sorrow, O hero, and give her a reply.
t.3.72.21: O wise one, speak once more that pleasing tale to her; the blameless Vaidarbhī wishes to hear those very words.
t.3.72.23: Bṛhadaśva said: O joy of the Kurus, when Nala had been addressed thus by Keśinī, his heart was pained and his eyes were filled with tears.
t.3.72.22: Having heard this, you reportedly gave him a reply. What you said before, Vaidarbhī wishes to hear again from you.
t.3.72.24: Restraining his own sorrow, the lord of the earth, burning with grief, spoke these words once more in a voice choked with tears.
t.3.72.25: Even when they have fallen into adversity, women of noble family guard themselves by their own selves; such virtuous women win heaven, there is no doubt.
t.3.72.26: Even when forsaken by their husbands, virtuous women never grow angry; shielded by the armor of their good conduct, they keep themselves alive in this world.
t.3.72.27: The dark one ought not to be angry with a man who, seeking merely to keep himself alive, had his garment carried off by birds and was being consumed by torments of the mind.
t.3.72.29: Speaking those words thus, Nala, deeply grieved, could not hold back his tears, and he wept aloud, O Bhārata.
t.3.72.28: Whether she is honored or dishonored, on seeing her husband in such a state, fallen from his kingdom, bereft of fortune, hungry, and overwhelmed by misfortune,
t.3.72.30: Then Keśinī went and reported to Damayantī all that had been said, and also that change that had come over him.
